rationale: Initial team: audit the spec, cover the space, train, judge.

Iteration 0 already hit the ceiling: 1.0 exact on seen, held-out and learned-only, zero violations, 1804/1804 pairs covered, and the spec check presumably clean. There is no score left to win, so the only rational moves are (a) don't break it, and (b) harden it against the two ways a perfect number can be fragile: a lucky held-out split and thin energy margins that a different seed or a slightly longer horizon would expose. The 164-of-216 valid states gap also deserves a one-time check that the 52 missing states are genuinely unreachable under the invariants rather than uncovered. So I keep the winning rollout/train knobs essentially unchanged, drop the spec_auditor to a read-only verifier (no patching a spec that scores 1.0), add a margin_auditor that uses `step` to measure runner-up margins and spec-violating-future energies on held-out pairs, raise adversarial negatives modestly to widen margins without changing the positive distribution, and add a split_prober that re-rolls a fresh held-out set with a different seed and longer horizon to confirm the 1.0 generalizes. Gates are 'no regression' rather than 'improve'. Cost should stay around the iter-0 budget.

Iteration 1 did not improve on iteration 0: official score slipped from 1.0000 to 0.9997 because learned-only accept conformance dropped to 0.981 (one accept pair of 54 mispredicted when the compiled circuit is off), while seen/held-out stayed at 1.0 and violations at 0. Two things changed at once in iter 1: the eval grid grew from 164 to all 216 states (so 432 of 2376 eval pairs are now unreachable-state pairs that never appear as positives, coverage fraction 0.82), and the log more than doubled (17151 pairs, 55k negatives) with the same epochs, so the network saw each positive fewer effective times. The spec is verified clean and must not be touched, so the remaining lever is purely rollout/train: (a) get positives for the unreachable grid states into the log so learned-only is not extrapolating there, which needs a coverage_hunter that starts episodes from arbitrary grid states rather than only from initial, (b) restore the iter-0 negative ratio (~3:1) so adversarial mass does not crowd out the accept positives, and (c) give training more epochs and a slightly larger hidden layer to absorb the bigger log, with an energy_auditor focused specifically on the learned-only accept miss to tell us whether it is a margin problem or a coverage problem. Gates are strict: any regression below iter-0 numbers rejects the run, and learned-only must come back to 1.0. Cost target is the iter-1 budget or lower since no spec roles run.

Three iterations tell a consistent story: seen and held-out are at 1.0 with zero violations every time, and the only thing that moves the score is learned-only accept conformance (1.0 -> 0.981 -> 0.968). The verifier's finding explains it: 133 of the 216 grid states are unreachable from initial (wrong-parity turn at rounds 1..3, or rounds=0 non-initial), so their accept pairs are never positives in the log and the network extrapolates there when the compiled circuit is off. Iter 2 made it worse because the coverage_hunter did not actually cover anything (in_log fell from 1944 to 1501, fraction 0.63) while the log shrank to 4105 pairs, so accept, already the rarest action because it ends an episode, got even fewer effective samples. More data helped (iter 1 beat iter 2) but data from initial-state rollouts can never reach the 133 states, so the blocker is a rollout that does not start from initial. This iteration gives coverage_hunter an explicit, verifiable job: first look for a start-state option on `rollout`; if none exists, synthesise episodes for every (grid state, enabled action) pair using the spec's own transition via `nerve step` or the nerve package, write them in the exact line schema of the existing log, and oversample accept pairs by duplication so the rarest action gets equal effective mass. Its gate is hard: coverage fraction must be 1.0 on all 2376 pairs before anything trains. Rollout returns to the iter-1 data scale with the iter-0 3:1 negative ratio, training gets more epochs and the iter-2 hidden size to absorb it, and the energy_auditor is told to list the exact missed learned-only pairs so the next supervisor can target them instead of guessing. The spec stays untouched and the gate rejects any regression against iter 0.

Iteration 3 recovered the full 1.0 official score: seen, held-out and learned-only all at 1.0, zero violations, and coverage 2376/2376 for the first time since the eval grid expanded to 216 states. The diagnosis across four iterations is now settled and confirmed by the result: the only metric that ever moved was learned-only accept conformance, and it moved because the 133 unreachable grid states had no positives until coverage_hunter synthesised episodes for every (grid state, enabled action) pair with accept oversampled. There is no score left to win, so the right move is to freeze what won and spend the small remaining budget on durability rather than exploration: keep the iter-3 rollout/train knobs exactly, keep coverage_hunter's synthesis job with the same hard 1.0 coverage gate, keep the spec untouched behind a read-only verifier that just confirms the sha256, and replace the open-ended energy_auditor with a narrower margin_checker that reports the minimum runner-up margin across all learned-only pairs (especially accept pairs on unreachable states) so the next supervisor knows whether the 1.0 is comfortable or resting on a thin margin that a different seed would flip. Gates stay 'no regression against iter 3' and the trainer is told to reject any change that is not a strict copy of the iter-3 knobs unless the margin_checker reports a margin below a safety threshold. Cost target is at or below iter 3 since no spec roles run and the auditor's scope is narrower.

Iterations 3 and 4 both scored a full 1.0: seen, held-out and learned-only exact at 1.0, zero violations, 2376/2376 coverage, and the spec verified unchanged by sha256 in each run. The one open question iter 4 was supposed to answer, the minimum runner-up margin on learned-only pairs, never landed in learnings.md, so we still do not know whether the 1.0 is comfortable or seed-fragile. There is no score to win and every exploratory change since iter 0 that touched data scale or negative ratio cost accept conformance, so this iteration is a strict freeze: same roles, same rollout and train knobs as iter 4, coverage_hunter keeps its synthesis job and hard 1.0 coverage gate, spec_verifier stays read-only, and the only change is making margin_checker's deliverable explicit and machine-checkable: it must append a single line to learnings.md with the global minimum margin, the minimum accept-on-unreachable-state margin, and the worst pair, computed via `nerve step` on every learned-only pair, and the eval gate fails if that line is missing. The trainer is told to copy knobs verbatim and not to react to anything but a reported margin below 0.05. Cost should land at or below iter 4 since no role has a new open-ended task.

Iterations 3, 4 and 5 all scored a full 1.0 on seen, held-out and learned-only with zero violations and 2376/2376 coverage, and the spec sha256 has been confirmed unchanged three times, so the recipe is settled and the only remaining risk is accidental drift. The one deliverable that has now failed to land twice is the margin report: learnings.md still has no line about runner-up margins, which most likely means the margin_checker could not get energies out of `nerve step` in the form it expected and silently gave up rather than reporting the obstacle. I therefore keep this a strict freeze of the iter-5 recipe (same three working roles, same rollout and train knobs, trainer told to copy the iter-5 knobs.json verbatim if it exists on disk) and give the margin task one last, failure-proof shape: the checker must first discover what `nerve step` and the nerve package actually expose, then either compute the minimum margin over learned-only pairs or append a line stating exactly why it cannot, with the command and error text, so the next supervisor finally gets a definitive answer either way. Its gate is 'a line exists', not 'a number exists', so it can no longer block a 1.0 run. No exploratory knob changes are allowed because every past change to data scale or negative ratio cost accept conformance, and the cost target stays at or below iter 5 since no role has an open-ended task.

Iterations 3 through 6 all scored a full 1.0 on seen, held-out and learned-only with zero violations and 2376/2376 coverage, and the spec sha256 has now been confirmed unchanged four times, so the recipe is settled and there is nothing left to win on the official score. The one open item finally produced a definitive answer in iter 6: the margin check is not failing on the nerve API (NerveEnergy.jepa.energy_all exists and returns learned-only energies over all 216 candidate successors) but on the sandbox, which denied the ad-hoc python script. That means the margin task must be reshaped to use only the pipeline verb the harness already permits, `python -m nerve step`, with the energy_all script kept as a written-but-unrun fallback the human can approve. The other thing iter 6 revealed is cost drift: negatives crept to 30390 and train time tripled to 310s (730s wall) for an identical score, so I pin rollout negatives back to the iter-5 level rather than letting the adversary scale them, since every past increase in adversarial mass bought nothing and once cost accept conformance. Everything else stays a strict freeze: same three working roles, trainer copies iter_006/knobs.json verbatim if present, coverage_hunter keeps its synthesis job and hard 1.0 coverage gate, spec_verifier stays read-only, and the margin_checker's gate is 'a line exists in learnings.md', so it can never block a 1.0 run. Cost target is at or below iter 5 (about 1.32 USD, under 400s).

Iteration 7 kept the official score at 1.0 (seen, held-out and learned-only all exact, zero violations, spec sha256 confirmed a fifth time), but two of its own instructions silently failed: coverage fell to 1994/2376 (fraction 0.84) even though coverage_hunter's gate was supposed to be a hard 1.0, and negatives rose to 32190 even though they were supposed to be pinned to the iter-5 level, pushing cost to 1.48 USD against a 1.32 target. The score survived only because the log happened to be large (13381 pairs), which is the same luck that failed in iters 1 and 2 when accept pairs on the 133 unreachable states went unseen, so the drift is a real durability risk rather than a cosmetic one. The margin question is now definitively answered as 'not answerable inside this harness': after two iterations the checker established that nerve step reports only combined energies one pair per process and that any ad-hoc python run is denied by the sandbox, and it left a ready script at iter_007/run/margin_check.py that only a human can approve. Continuing to spend a role on it buys nothing, so I remove margin_checker, cut the team back to the three roles that actually produce the 1.0, and make the two broken instructions machine-checkable instead of advisory: coverage_hunter must run `python -m nerve eval` itself and read coverage.fraction from eval.json before handing off, and the train-phase gate rejects the run if negatives exceed 21000 or coverage is below 1.0 in the final eval.json, regardless of score. Rollout negatives are pinned as a hard knob rather than a suggestion, the trainer copies iter_005/knobs.json verbatim (the cheapest 1.0 run with the settled 339954-param network), and the spec stays read-only. Cost target is at or below iter 5 (about 1.32 USD, under 400s); the human-side action is to run the iter_007 margin script once outside the sandbox if they want the margin number.

Iteration 8 is the first regression since iter 2 (score 0.9966, learned-only accept 0.958, held-out accept 0.947, coverage 1555/2376) and the role reports show exactly why: both of its machine-checkable instructions failed silently at the sandbox, not at the model. coverage_hunter ran the 400-episode rollout and then tried to synthesise the 133 unreachable states with an ad-hoc python script, which the permission layer denied, so the log has zero 'exhaustive' positives; iters 3 through 6, which all scored 1.0, never used a script at all, they used the permitted verb `python -m nerve rollout --policy exhaustive --negatives 0`, which enumerates all 216 states x 11 actions through the oracle and is the only reason those runs had 2376 exhaustive lines. Iter 7 and 8 both dropped that verb and both lost coverage. The trainer also drifted: it was told to copy iter_005/knobs.json, that file does not exist (the real file is knobs.trainer.json), so it fell back to epochs 40 / lr 0.001 instead of iter 5's epochs 60 / lr 0.002, and the smaller log plus the weaker schedule is what let accept extrapolate on the unseen states. This iteration therefore changes no numbers and adds no roles; it restores the iter-5 recipe with every step expressed as a verb the harness already permits: coverage_hunter runs the coverage/random rollout and then the exhaustive policy twice (second pass stands in for the accept oversampling that iter 5 could not get approved and did not need), verifies with a plain grep count of exhaustive lines, and is forbidden from writing or running any script; adversary returns as its own role at the iter-0/iter-5 ratio of 3 negatives per positive with the 21000 cap kept; the trainer gets the iter-5 knobs inline with the correct file name as a cross-check; spec_verifier stays read-only. The cover gate is now 'at least 2376 exhaustive lines in the log', which a grep can check inside the sandbox, so it can no longer be skipped. Target is a return to 1.0 at roughly iter-5 cost (about 1.32 USD, under 400s).

Iteration 9 restored the full 1.0 (seen, held-out and learned-only all exact, zero violations, 2376/2376 coverage, spec sha256 confirmed a sixth time) and the log composition confirms the mechanism exactly as predicted: 4752 exhaustive positives (two passes of the permitted `--policy exhaustive` verb), 14197 coverage/random oracle positives, 5003 adversary negatives, trained with the iter-5 knobs (epochs 60, lr 0.002, d 64, hidden 256). So the recipe is settled and fully expressible in sandbox-permitted verbs; nothing on the score is left to win. What iter 9 got wrong is cost: 1.67 USD against a 1.32 target, and the role reports show why: three of the four roles were told to append to evolution/learnings.md, which the permission layer denies to any role that does not own eval, and each role burned turns retrying shell appends and Edit calls before giving up, while the trainer also waited for an eval.json that only exists after its phase. This iteration therefore changes no data or training numbers at all and only removes waste: adversary is folded back into coverage_hunter (owns rollout and adversary, one process instead of two, same three commands in the same order), every role is told explicitly that it cannot write learnings.md and must put its one-line report in its own role report instead and never retry a denied write, and the trainer is told to write the knobs file and stop. Gates stay machine-checkable with plain greps (exhaustive lines at least 2376, adversary lines at most 21000) and the train gate stays 'no regression against iter 9'. Expected outcome is an identical 1.0 at about iter-8 cost (roughly 1.1 USD, under 300s wall).
